title: Holi: the festival of colors
hookLine: little Krishna colors Radha's face; in Braj, Holi is his divine play, and everyone joins in
carry: holi is krishna's play, and everyone's invited

lines: WHY IS SHE FAIR AND I'M DARK?
cards: A little boy runs to his mother, upset. Why is Radha so fair, he asks, and I'm so dark? It isn't fair.
His mother, smiling, has an idea. Go and color her face, she says, any color you like. Then you'll match.
The boy is Krishna, the mother Yashoda, and that small story, told and sung all over the Braj country where Krishna grew up, is one of the reasons people there say Holi began.

teach.b: Braj is the region around Mathura and Vrindavan, south of Delhi, where Krishna's childhood stories are set. In Braj, Holi isn't one day; it's a season of a week or more.
In Barsana, the village tradition remembers as Radha's, there's Lathmar Holi, Holi of the sticks.
Men from Nandgaon, Krishna's village, come over to throw color, and the women of Barsana meet them with long sticks, playfully beating them while the men hide under shields and everyone sings.
The next day, it happens the other way around in Nandgaon. In Vrindavan's temples, there's a day when priests throw flower petals over the crowd.
Many families tell two stories: the fire the night before, for Prahlad, and the colors the next day, which in Braj belong to Krishna. Now the teaching.
Hindus have a word for what Krishna does in Braj: lila, divine play. The God who holds the universe steals butter, teases his mother, and throws color.
And in Braj devotion, Radha's love for Krishna is the model of bhakti: loving God the way you love the person closest to you, with joy, not fear. That's why Holi there isn't a show to watch.
Everyone joins the play, young and old, rich and poor, Barsana and Nandgaon. Under the color, nobody can tell who's who.
Many devotees read that as the point: in Krishna's play, the faces are level, and everyone's invited in.

how: In the Braj region around Mathura and Vrindavan, Holi is celebrated over a week or more, with Lathmar Holi in Barsana and Nandgaon, flower Holi in Vrindavan's temples, and songs of Krishna and Radha; elsewhere many families tell both Prahlad's story and Krishna's.

games.q: a cousin says a paint fight can't be real worship. by Braj's teaching, what fits?
o: in Braj, the play is the worship: Holi joins Krishna's lila, and loving God can be joyful.
true; the colors are just fun, and the worship happens separately.
only the priests' flower petals count as worship.
games.why: lila means divine play. in Braj bhakti, loving Krishna with joy is the point, not a break from it.

practice: In Vrindavan, people greet each other with two words: Radhe Radhe. Think of someone you feel slightly apart from: a different age, different politics, a different background.
Picture both your faces covered in the same bright pink powder, so nobody could say which is which. If you pray, say Radhe Radhe for them, silently. If you don't, just wish them well.
Let any small grudge slide off with the color.

wordCard.voice: Holi. In Braj it's Krishna's lila, his season of play, with sticks in Barsana and petals in Vrindavan, and every face the same bright mess.

orig.note: Hindi lāṭhī (stick) + mār (beat) + holī: Barsana's Holi of the sticks.
